question: A clock chimes once at \(30\) minutes past each hour and chimes on the hour according to the hour. For example, at \(1\) PM there is one chime and at noon and midnight there are twelve chimes. Starting at \(11{:}15\) AM on February \(26,\) \(2003,\) on what date will the \(2003\)rd chime occur?
solution:
The chime schedule repeats every day, so first count one day's chimes. In each twelve hours, the on-the-hour chimes total
\[
1+2+\cdots+12=6\cdot13=78,
\]
where pairing \(1\) with \(12\), \(2\) with \(11\), and so on gives six pairs of \(13\). A full day has two such sets and \(24\) single half-hour chimes, for a total of
\[
2\cdot78+24=180.
\]
This also counts the chimes from 11:15 AM one day to 11:15 AM the next, since the schedule repeats and neither endpoint is a chiming time.

Now
\[
2003=11\cdot180+23.
\]
Thus, after eleven complete days, \(1980\) chimes have occurred and we need \(23\) more. February has \(28\) days in \(2003\): three days after February \(26\) is March \(1\), and eight more days brings us to March \(9\), at 11:15 AM.

From then through 12:30 PM, there are \(1+12+1=14\) chimes. From 1 PM through 3:30 PM, the hourly and following half-hour chimes add
\[
(1+1)+(2+1)+(3+1)=9.
\]
These give the remaining \(14+9=23\) chimes. The \(2003\)rd chime occurs at 3:30 PM on \(\boxed{\text{March }9}\), choice \(\text{B}\).
